name: Requests users never meant to send (CSRF)

slides.title: How CSRF works
slides.summary: Another site makes the user's browser send a request to yours, and the browser attaches the user's cookies.
body: Browsers attach cookies based on where a request is going, not where it came from. A malicious page can submit a form to your site, and the logged-in user's session cookie goes with it.
The attacker can't read the response (the same-origin policy stops that), but they don't need to: the damage is the action itself.
<mark>Any state-changing request authenticated only by cookies is a CSRF target.</mark>

body.note: Using GET for actions (/delete?id=5) makes it worse: an <img> tag is enough to trigger it.

body.text: Forging the login form signs the victim into the attacker's account. Anything they then save (cards, searches) goes to the attacker. Protect login forms too.

figure.alt: Top row, the attack: a page on evil.example contains a hidden form that auto-submits a POST to bank.example/transfer. The browser attaches the user's session cookie for bank.example, and the bank, seeing a valid session, performs the transfer. Bottom row, defended: the same forged POST arrives, but the cookie is SameSite=Lax so the browser does not attach it on a cross-site POST, and the request carries Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site, which the server rejects; a CSRF token check would also fail because the attacker cannot read the token.

slides.title: Why CSRF is possible
slides.summary: HTTP is stateless and cookies ride along automatically, so the server can't tell a request the user meant from one another site triggered.
body: Each HTTP request stands alone. The server recognises the user only by the credentials that arrive with it, and the browser adds cookies automatically. Many ordinary HTML features can trigger a cross-site request:

ul: An image: <img src="https://forum.example/posts/9/delete"> fires a GET as soon as the page or email loads.
A link in a chat message or email, clicked in a hurry.
An auto-submitting form that POSTs as soon as the page opens, possibly in a hidden iframe.
A fetch with credentials: 'include' using a simple content type.

body: <mark>Any endpoint that changes state using only cookie authentication, and accepts a request a plain HTML page can send, is a CSRF target.</mark>

body.note: A forum that deletes posts with GET /posts/9/delete can be attacked by an image in any web page or HTML email the moderator opens. State changes must never use GET.

slides.title: Defending against CSRF
slides.summary: SameSite cookies are the baseline. Add a Fetch Metadata or Origin check, and tokens for anything sensitive.

ul: SameSite cookies: Lax withholds cookies on cross-site POSTs, iframes and fetch; Strict also drops them on cross-site links. Set it explicitly: only Chromium defaults to Lax.

Fetch Metadata: reject unsafe methods when Sec-Fetch-Site is cross-site (all major browsers send it). Go 1.25's CrossOriginProtection does exactly this. Fall back to an Origin check when the header is missing.
CSRF tokens: a random value tied to the session, sent in a header or hidden field. A cross-site page can't read it, so it can't include it.

body: <mark>SameSite protects against other sites, not your own subdomains. A compromised subdomain is same-site, so pair it with tokens or origin checks.</mark>

body.text: Angular's HttpClient reads an XSRF-TOKEN cookie and sends it as an X-XSRF-TOKEN header on mutating same-origin requests (the double-submit pattern). Configure names with withXsrfConfiguration(); the server sets the cookie and checks they match.

slides.title: The synchronizer token pattern
slides.summary: The server issues a random per-session token; the page sends it back with every state change; the server compares before acting.
body: A CSRF token works because the attacker's page can make the browser send a request, but can't read your pages to learn the token.

ul: Generate it with a secure random generator (32 bytes) and store it with the server-side session.
Put it in the page (a <meta> tag or hidden field), or a readable cookie for the double-submit variant.
Send it back in a custom header (X-CSRF-Token) on every POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE.
Compare with a constant-time function, and reject with 403 if it's missing or wrong.
Rotate it at login, and never put it in a URL, where it leaks through logs and Referer headers.

body: <mark>Checking the token in the browser does nothing: the attacker's request never runs your JavaScript. The server must check it.</mark>

ul: Origin / Referer check: compare against an exact allowlist with new URL(), not startsWith (which https://shop.example.evil.example passes).
Re-authentication or a one-time code before high-value actions such as payouts.
CAPTCHA slows automated abuse of forms, but isn't a CSRF defence on its own.

code: const ok = sent.length === expected.length && crypto.timingSafeEqual(sent, expected);

figure.alt: A sequence between the browser tab on shop.example, the shop server, and an attacker page on evil.example. 1: the page loads; the server creates a random token, stores it with the session, and embeds it in the page or a cookie. 2: when the user changes their address, the page sends the request with the session cookie plus the token in a header or hidden field. 3: the server compares the token with the one stored for the session using a constant-time comparison, and the request succeeds. 4: evil.example forges the same request; the browser attaches the session cookie, but the attacker could not read the token, because the same-origin policy stops it reading shop.example pages. 5: the server sees a missing or wrong token and returns 403.
